subject: crab
reasoning:
I'm planning out the crab model structure using the SDK, reviewing the builder's joint API and its parameters like parent, position, aim, and grouping before writing the TypeScript module.

Still cataloging API functions...

The module needs to return the root group after assembly. I'm thinking through art direction: a stylized, puppet-like crab with bold primitives, probably a red-orange shore crab around 0.2m wide with a pale underside and dark eye stalks, keeping the look bold and blocky. For anatomy, I'm considering using a lathe shape for the flattened dome carapace, figuring out which axis to spin it around to get the wide, flat proportions right.

Since the lathe is axis-symmetric, it can't give the carapace its wide, flattened shape, so scaling a sphere non-uniformly seems more practical. Actually, extruding a crab-shaped outline in plan view with thickness tapering along the vertical axis could work well — setting up the extrude orientation so the outline sits in the XZ plane and thickness runs along Y.

Thinking through it more, a scaled sphere is the simpler approach: something like radius-1 sphere scaled to roughly 0.2 wide, 0.07 tall, 0.15 long to match realistic crab proportions. I need to figure out how high to position the carapace so the legs hold it above the ground properly, with the legs' tips and lowest points touching the floor.

Now I'm working out concrete dimensions for a stylized but real-world-sized crab: carapace around 0.2m wide, 0.14m long, 0.075m tall, with legs spanning out to about 0.5m, and placing the body center roughly 0.12m above the ground.

I'm designing each of the four walking leg pairs as a joint chain (hip, knee, ankle, foot) using a polyline path through key points, so the legs splay outward and the last segments angle down to touch the floor at y≈0.

I'm weighing whether to skin each leg chain with a smooth sweep for a tapered tube look, or build rigid segment-by-segment capsules/rods for a more blocky puppet aesthetic, leaning toward sweeping over the chain since it naturally bends at the joints.

I'm placing cylinder geometry along each segment's direction, centered at the midpoint, with the bone assigned explicitly to the correct joint.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy — deciding whether the root should be a body joint, and whether roles like "leg", "spine", or "hinge" apply to this crab rig's structure.

For the crab specifically, I'm assigning "leg" to the walking legs and "arm" to the claw chains, and considering whether eye stalks need a distinct role or can be left unassigned. I'm also weighing whether to give the claw's pincer a "jaw" role with a hinge axis, which would require getting the joint's local X orientation right via the dir/up aiming so the pincer opens correctly.

For the claw arm chain, I'm structuring it as shoulder-elbow-wrist joints with a hand tip, plus a separate moving finger joint with a "jaw" role for the pincer action. Now I'm thinking through the carapace design — a red-orange mottled sphere with a rostrum spikes up front, and eye stalks as short capsule joints topped with black eyeball spheres.

For the mouth area, I'm considering a simple pale slab or small palp shapes beneath the front, and for the abdomen I'm planning a flat triangular cream-colored plate tucked under the rear of the carapace, positioned so it's only partly visible from below or behind, true to how a real crab's tail flap folds under its shell.

Now I'm thinking through the walking legs: four pairs attached along the lower edge of the carapace at staggered positions, each leg built from three simplified segments (thigh, shin, foot) extending outward and down to meet the ground, with the tips sinking slightly below the body for grounding.

Checking the math, hip at y=0.1 sits right at the carapace surface, which works well. For the leg geometry I'm thinking of each leg lifting up slightly at the knee then descending through the ankle to touch the ground, with the hip, knee, ankle, and foot positions offset outward and backward per leg to keep proportions crab-like.

Rather than computing each joint by hand, I'll generalize it with a function that takes a side and leg index and returns the four joint positions, with per-pair arrays controlling the forward/back hip offset, outward reach, and foot placement so the front legs angle forward and the back legs angle backward.

Total leg reach from hip is about 0.2 for good extension. I'm deciding on leg thickness, tapering from a thicker radius near the hip to a thinner one at the tip, and weighing whether to build the segments as capsule sweeps rigidly bound to each joint bone versus using cylinder geometry parts for a more controlled, low-poly look.

Writing segment helper function...

Now I'm thinking through how to rig the leg joints using a chain structure — naming each joint (hip, knee, ankle, foot) and ensuring the chain correctly aims each segment at the next point, with the parent joint connecting back to the body.

I'm deciding that using b.chain is simpler than manually creating each joint, since it automatically handles the "leg" role and keeps everything connected properly for the rig.

For the leg pieces themselves, I'm planning cylinder segments with small sphere knuckles at the knee and ankle joints, bone-bound to those joints for natural bending. I'm also considering adding a subtle stripe paint pattern across the legs for visual texture, while being mindful that too many painted parts will reduce texel density on the shared paint sheet, and now I'm settling on a color palette starting with a deep red-orange shell tone with darker and lighter variants.

Now I'm working out the rest of the palette: cream for the belly and claw tips, black eyes, dark claw tip accents, and a subtle cream-on-red stripe pattern for the legs -- but I'm realizing stripe bands are oriented in world space along a chosen axis, so rings around an X-oriented leg would look right with axis "x", though each leg points a different direction, so the striping would look oblique rather than clean rings on most legs.

For the legs I'll just go with solid colouring plus painted claw tips rather than fighting the diagonal orientation issue. For the shell, I'm planning a spotted paint with a darker red base and reddish-brown spots, layered with countershading so the carapace dome reads darker on top and lighter toward the belly, using the surface normal's vertical component to blend the two tones.

The claws will share the shell's warm red-orange colouring, but I want to give the fingertips a dark near-black tip for readability, so I'm thinking of either a separate small capsule piece or a painted gradient near the tip to create that contrast.

Now I'm working out the claw's geometry: a jointed arm from shoulder to elbow to wrist to hand, positioned forward and outward from the carapace's front, then a bulbous palm shape with a fixed finger extending forward and a moving finger hinged at the palm base so it can pivot to meet the fixed one, like a real crab chela.

I'm thinking of making each finger a flat, tapering extruded outline in the horizontal plane with thickness along the vertical axis, going from a wide base to a pointed tip to get that pincer look.

For the moving finger, I'm positioning its outline at the pivot joint facing forward, and figuring out the right axis for `pose` so rotating that joint about the world Y axis convincingly opens and closes the claw.

The geometry placement doesn't actually need to match the joint orientation for rigging purposes—only the hinge axis matters for the rig. For the claw itself, I'm thinking through where the fingers extend from the palm: the arm points mostly forward with slight outward lean, and the pincer fingers should pivot around a shared axis, with the fixed finger on the outer edge and the moving finger positioned to close against it.

Defining finger outlines...

I'll keep the moving finger as a simple convex triangle shape angled toward the fixed finger, so the tips roughly meet to form the pincer. Then I'll add small black spheres at each tip to represent the claw's pointed ends.

Now I'm working out the arm skeleton: placing joints for shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand, then connecting them with bone segments and adding small knuckle spheres at the elbow and wrist. I'm also figuring out where the palm sphere sits relative to the hand joint, and planning the pincer joint as a child of the hand to drive the claw's opening motion.

For symmetry, I'm building a mirror function so I only need to define one side of the crab and reflect it for the other, deciding to keep both claws roughly the same size rather than making one a crusher and one a cutter, since that asymmetry could introduce bugs. I'm now thinking through how to mirror the claw outline geometry correctly by flipping the x-coordinates for the right side.

Tallying up the part count: body, rostrum, lateral spikes, eight legs with knee and ankle joints, claws with knuckles and fingers, eye stalks, and the abdomen slab — roughly 80 parts total, comfortably under the triangle budget. I'm setting up the pincer joint's hinge axis using a consistent up vector so both left and right claws rotate correctly, and placing a shared black tip sphere where the fingers meet.
